🥪 Digestive System → Hydrolysis & Fiber

Indicator HS20-NU1a, d

What You Learned: Salivary amylase, pepsin, pancreatic lipases, and brush-border enzymes chemically digest food so small intestine villi can absorb nutrients, while the colon reabsorbs water.
Leg 1 Nutrition Connection: Whole food polymers (starch, proteins, triglycerides) are too gigantic to cross the epithelial membrane of your intestinal villi! Your digestive enzymes must use water (hydrolysis) to split them into monomers (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids). Meanwhile, indigestible soluble and insoluble fiber regulate gastric emptying speed and colonic peristalsis.

Step 2A • Route Info Schema Builder (Indicator HS20-NU1a)

Water, Monomers & Biological Polymers

🔗 SK Curriculum HS20-NU1 🔗 SK HS20 Nutrition Notes (Petlak) 🎥 Watch: Crash Course Biomolecules

📖 Science Primer 1A: Read This First

1. Why Water (H2O) Is Essential: Water accounts for 60–70% of human body weight. Even a 2% loss of body water impairs athletic and cognitive performance. In human physiology, water serves 5 critical functions:

  • Universal Solvent & Transport: Dissolves glucose, amino acids, electrolytes, and O2 in blood plasma (which is 92% water).
  • Thermoregulation: Absorbs metabolic heat and cools the body via evaporation of sweat.
  • Lubrication & Cushioning: Forms synovial fluid in joints, mucus in the GI tract, and cerebrospinal fluid around the brain.
  • Cell Volume & Osmolarity: Maintains intracellular pressure for nerve and muscle function.
  • Direct Chemical Reactant: Consumed directly to split food bonds during digestion (hydrolysis)!

2. Monomers vs. Polymers: Think of a monomer as a single LEGO brick (e.g., 1 glucose sugar or 1 amino acid) and a polymer as a long castle wall built from hundreds of bricks linked by covalent bonds (e.g., starch, glycogen, or a muscle protein).

Simple vs. Complex Carbohydrates (4 kcal/g)

Carbohydrates are your body's preferred short-term energy source—especially for your brain (which relies almost exclusively on glucose) and high-intensity muscular contractions.

⚡ Simple Carbohydrates (Monosaccharides & Disaccharides)

Monosaccharides (1 ring): Glucose (blood sugar), Fructose (fruit sugar), Galactose.
Disaccharides (2 rings): Sucrose (glucose + fructose = table sugar), Lactose (glucose + galactose = milk sugar), Maltose (glucose + glucose).
Physiology: Require zero or minimal hydrolysis—absorb rapidly in minutes, causing a sharp rise in blood glucose and a heavy pancreas insulin spike.

🔋 Complex Carbohydrates (Polysaccharides: Starch & Glycogen)

Plant Starch (Amylose/Amylopectin): Found in oats, wild rice, barley, quinoa, potatoes, and Saskatchewan lentils/peas. Hundreds of glucose units take time for amylase enzymes to hydrolyze, giving a slow, steady release of glucose.
Human Glycogen: Your body stores ~100 g of glycogen in the liver (to maintain blood glucose between meals) and ~400 g in skeletal muscles (for exercise ATP).

🔗 Health Canada: Carbohydrates 🔗 Diabetes Canada: Glycemic Index Guide

Why We Need Indigestible Plant Fiber (HS20-NU1d)

Dietary fiber consists of plant polysaccharides (like cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin, and beta-glucan) linked by beta-glycosidic bonds that human digestive enzymes cannot break. Even though it provides almost zero calories (0–2 kcal/g from gut microbiome fermentation), Health Canada recommends 25–38 g/day for optimal health:

💧 Soluble Fiber ("The Gel Sponge")

Dissolves in water to form a viscous gel in the stomach and small intestine.

1. Glycemic Control: Slows gastric emptying so glucose absorbs gradually (lowering Glycemic Index).

2. Lowers LDL Cholesterol: Binds bile acids (made from cholesterol) in the small intestine and excretes them, forcing the liver to pull LDL out of the blood!

Sources: Oats (beta-glucan), flaxseed, chia, psyllium, lentils, apples, saskatoon berries.

🌾 Insoluble Fiber ("The Gut Broom")

Does not dissolve in water; remains intact through the entire GI tract.

1. Prevents Constipation: Adds physical bulk and attracts water into stool, stimulating smooth muscle peristalsis in the colon (maintaining healthy Bristol Stool Chart Types 3–4).

2. Diverticular & Colon Health: Reduces intraluminal pressure and speeds transit of waste.

Sources: Whole wheat bran, brown/wild rice hulls, celery, broccoli, seed skins.

⚠️ R&D Formulation Warning: Timing Fiber Around Exercise!

When engineering your supplement, you must match your fiber content to when your client consumes it:

  • Daily Meal Replacement Bar / Shake (5–9 g Fiber): High soluble + insoluble fiber is ideal here! It keeps a busy farmer, student, or hospital patient full for 4 hours, prevents blood sugar spikes, and lowers LDL cholesterol.
  • Mid-Race Isotonic Sports Drink (0–1 g Fiber): Putting 10 g of fiber into a mid-marathon sports drink is a disaster! Fiber slows gastric emptying and ferments in the colon, causing sloshing, gas, and runner's GI cramps when blood flow is shunted away from the gut to working leg muscles.

Lipids (9 kcal/g) & Lipoprotein Transport (HS20-NU1e)

Lipids provide dense long-term energy storage (9 kcal/g), insulate organs, form the phospholipid bilayer of every cell membrane and neuron myelin sheath, build steroid hormones (testosterone, estrogen, cortisol), and are required to absorb fat-soluble Vitamins A, D, E, and K.

✅ Unsaturated Fats (Mono- & Polyunsaturated Omega-3 / Omega-6): Contain 1 or more C=C double bonds that put a physical "kink" in the fatty acid chain so they stay liquid at room temperature (flaxseed oil, olive oil, canola, avocado, walnuts, salmon). Raises HDL ("Healthy") and lowers LDL ("Lousy").
⚠️ Saturated Fats (Animal Fats & Tropical Oils): Zero double bonds—straight chains pack tightly as solids at room temperature (butter, lard, fatty beef/bacon, palm/coconut oil). Excess intake downregulates liver LDL receptors, raising blood LDL cholesterol.
🚫 Artificial Trans Fats (Partially Hydrogenated Oils): Industrially straightened unsaturated oils (banned in Canada since 2018). Double whammy: spikes LDL AND destroys protective HDL, accelerating coronary atherosclerosis.
🔗 Heart & Stroke: Managing HDL & LDL Cholesterol 🔗 Heart & Stroke: Dietary Fats & Oils

🩸 LDL vs. HDL Cholesterol: The Artery Transport Battle

Because cholesterol is hydrophobic (insoluble in watery blood plasma), your liver wraps it in protein shells called lipoproteins. Memorize this distinction for your Pit Stop oral defense:

LDL = Low-Density Lipoprotein ("Lousy")

Direction: Carries cholesterol from the liver out to body tissues and arteries.

Pathology: Excess LDL oxidizes and burrows under damaged arterial endothelium, forming hard atherosclerotic plaque that narrows coronary arteries (heart attack) or cerebral arteries (stroke).

HDL = High-Density Lipoprotein ("Healthy")

Direction: Acts as an arterial garbage truck—scavenges excess cholesterol from artery walls back to the liver for excretion in bile!

How to Boost HDL: Aerobic exercise, omega-3 & monounsaturated fats (flax, hemp, olive oil), and soluble fiber.

Proteins (4 kcal/g) & Essential Amino Acids (HS20-NU1f)

Proteins are the structural and functional machinery of human cells—forming skeletal muscle actin and myosin, connective tissue collagen, digestive enzymes, red blood cell hemoglobin, peptide hormones (insulin), and immune antibodies.

  • 20 Total Amino Acids: Linked by peptide bonds during ribosomal translation.
  • 11 Non-Essential Amino Acids: Your liver can synthesize these via transamination.
  • 9 Essential Amino Acids (EAAs): Histidine, Isoleucine, Leucine, Lysine, Methionine, Phenylalanine, Threonine, Tryptophan, and Valine. Your body cannot make them—they must come from food! (Leucine is the key Branched-Chain Amino Acid [BCAA] that switches on muscle protein synthesis after exercise).
  • Complete vs. Incomplete Proteins: Animal foods (whey, milk, eggs, beef, bison, fish) plus soy, quinoa, buckwheat, and hemp seeds contain all 9 EAAs in adequate amounts. Most single plant foods have a "limiting amino acid" (legumes/pulses are low in Methionine; grains/seeds are low in Lysine).
🔗 Health Canada: Protein & Amino Acids 🔗 Khan Academy: Proteins & Peptide Bonds

📐 How the 4-4-9 Rule Works (Partner A Reference Guide):

Every gram of macronutrient releases a specific amount of physiological energy when oxidized in cellular respiration: Digestible Carbs (Starch + Sugars) = 4 kcal/g • Protein = 4 kcal/g • Fat (Lipids) = 9 kcal/g • Dietary Fiber & Sugar Alcohols (Polyols) = ~1.5 kcal/g (only partially fermented in the colon). Option A Guide: Engineering a 'Slow Burn' Glycemic Matrix

1. Dual-Stage Carb Blend: Pair a slow-digesting complex starch (rolled oats, barley, lentil flour, wild rice) with a modest amount of natural fruit sugar (saskatoon berries, dates) for immediate + 3-hour ATP.
2. Soluble Fiber Gel (4–8 g): Use oat beta-glucan, ground flaxseed, or chia seeds to form a viscous gel in the small intestine that blunts the post-meal glucose spike.
3. Moderate Protein & Lipid Anchor: Include 12–18 g protein and 6–10 g unsaturated fat to further slow gastric emptying without causing heavy stomach cramping.
